prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) -- Five members of the Sri Lanka's Civil Defense Force (CDF) were killed in a suicide blast in Sri Lanka at a church outside the capital of Colombo Sunday morning, police said. Sri Lankan police officers investigate Sunday's suicide bombing near Colombo. Eight other CDF officers and two civilians were wounded, police said. Nobody immediately claimed responsibility for the blast, but police suspect the bomber was a member of the Tamil Tiger rebels. There was no immediate response from the Tamil Tiger rebels to the incident, which, police said, occurred at St. Anne's Church in the Colombo suburb of Wattala, located on a roadway to the country's only international airport about 15 kilometers (9 miles) north of the capital. The attack happened during a weekly festival that usually draws a large crowd shopping for vegetables and household goods. The suicide bomber walked into an area where CDF officers were stationed and detonated his explosives, police said. Investigators suspect the bomber targeted the area because 150 police officers who help patrol the road to the airport are billeted there. Government forces have engaged rebels in heavy fighting for more than a year in the Kilinochchi region, once the center of political power for the Tamil Tigers. The 25-year civil war between ethnic Tamil separatists and the Sri Lankan government has left more than 65,000 people dead. The Tamil Tigers were founded in 1976, and the U.S. State Department designated the group a foreign terrorist organization in 1997. The rebels, formally known as the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), are fighting for the creation of an independent nation, citing discrimination by the country's Sinhalese majority. Earlier Sunday, Sri Lanka's navy said it had destroyed a Tamil Tiger rebel boat allegedly attempting to smuggle in military supplies through the northern coast. Commander D.K.P. Dissanayake, a navy spokesman, told CNN that four rebels were killed in attack after the boat was engulfed in fire. He said the incident occurred just after midnight Sunday but gave no other details. There was no immediate response from the Tiger rebels to that incident. CNN could not independently verify the government's claim because media is debarred from Sri Lanka's battle zones. In the past, both sides in the conflict have exaggerated accounts of military operations. On December 20, the Navy said it destroyed a similar rebel boat trying to smuggle military supplies through the coast near the northeastern coastal village of Mullaitivu. However, a second supply boat was caught on Air Force aerial surveillance cameras unloading along the coast. "They included assorted ammunition, artillery shells, mortar shells and other items," a senior Air Force official told CNN. He spoke on grounds of anonymity since he was not authorized to speak to the media.

outputs.L1:
**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) —** Five members of Sri Lanka’s Civil Defense Force (CDF) were killed in a suicide bombing at a church outside the capital, Colombo, on Sunday morning, police said.

Sri Lankan police officers investigated the scene of Sunday’s suicide bombing near Colombo. Eight other CDF officers and two civilians were wounded, according to police.

No one immediately claimed responsibility for the blast, but police suspect the bomber was a member of the Tamil Tiger rebels. The group did not immediately respond to the incident.

Police said the bombing occurred at St. Anne’s Church in the Colombo suburb of Wattala, along a road leading to the country’s only international airport, about 15 kilometers (9 miles) north of the capital.

The attack took place during a weekly festival that typically draws large crowds shopping for vegetables and household goods. The suicide bomber entered an area where CDF officers were stationed and detonated his explosives, police said.

Investigators suspect the bomber targeted the area because 150 police officers who help patrol the road to the airport are billeted there.

Government forces have been engaged in heavy fighting with rebels for more than a year in the Kilinochchi region, once the center of political power for the Tamil Tigers.

The 25-year civil war between ethnic Tamil separatists and the Sri Lankan government has left more than 65,000 people dead.

The Tamil Tigers were founded in 1976, and the U.S. State Department designated the group a foreign terrorist organization in 1997. Formally known as the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), the rebels are fighting to establish an independent nation, citing discrimination by the country’s Sinhalese majority.

Earlier Sunday, Sri Lanka’s navy said it had destroyed a Tamil Tiger rebel boat that was allegedly attempting to smuggle military supplies through the northern coast.

Commander D.K.P. Dissanayake, a navy spokesman, told CNN that four rebels were killed in the attack after the boat was engulfed in flames. He said the incident occurred shortly after midnight Sunday but provided no further details.

The Tamil Tiger rebels did not immediately respond to that incident.

CNN could not independently verify the government’s claim because the media are barred from Sri Lanka’s battle zones. Both sides in the conflict have previously exaggerated accounts of military operations.

On December 20, the navy said it had destroyed a similar rebel boat that was attempting to smuggle military supplies through the coast near the northeastern village of Mullaitivu.

However, a second supply boat was captured by Air Force aerial surveillance cameras unloading cargo along the coast.

“They included assorted ammunition, artillery shells, mortar shells and other items,” a senior Air Force official told CNN. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.
outputs.L2:
COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) — A suicide bombing at a church near Sri Lanka’s capital killed five members of the country’s Civil Defense Force on Sunday morning, according to police.

Authorities said eight other CDF personnel and two civilians were injured. Sri Lankan police officers examined the scene of the attack, which took place at St. Anne’s Church in Wattala, a Colombo suburb. Wattala lies along the road leading to Sri Lanka’s only international airport, roughly 15 kilometers (9 miles) north of the capital.

No group immediately took responsibility, although police believe the attacker may have belonged to the Tamil Tiger rebel movement. The rebels did not immediately comment on the bombing.

The explosion occurred during a weekly festival that normally attracts many people buying vegetables and household supplies. Police said the bomber entered an area occupied by CDF officers and set off the explosives. Investigators believe the site may have been chosen because it houses 150 police officers assigned to help secure the airport road.

For more than a year, government troops and rebel forces have been involved in intense combat in Kilinochchi, formerly the Tamil Tigers’ political stronghold. The 25-year civil war between the Sri Lankan government and ethnic Tamil separatists has killed more than 65,000 people.

Established in 1976, the Tamil Tigers were classified as a foreign terrorist organization by the U.S. State Department in 1997. Officially called the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, the group seeks an independent state, arguing that Tamils face discrimination from Sri Lanka’s Sinhalese majority.

In a separate development earlier Sunday, the Sri Lankan navy reported destroying a Tamil Tiger vessel that it said was trying to bring military supplies into the country through the northern coastline.

Navy spokesman Commander D.K.P. Dissanayake told CNN that the boat caught fire during the attack and that four rebels died. He said the confrontation happened shortly after midnight Sunday but provided no further information. The Tamil Tigers also offered no immediate reaction to that event.

Because journalists are prohibited from entering Sri Lanka’s combat areas, CNN was unable to independently confirm the government’s account. Both the government and the rebels have previously overstated claims about battlefield operations.

On December 20, the navy reported destroying another rebel vessel that was allegedly attempting to transport military equipment through waters near Mullaitivu, a coastal village in the northeast. A second supply boat, however, was recorded by Air Force aerial-surveillance cameras unloading material on the shore.

A senior Air Force official said the cargo consisted of various types of ammunition, artillery rounds, mortar shells and additional supplies. The official requested anonymity because he was not permitted to speak with the media.

# Colombo, Sri Lanka: A Vibrant Coastal Capital

Colombo is the largest city and commercial capital of Sri Lanka. Located on the island’s western coast, it combines modern skyscrapers, colonial architecture, lively markets, and peaceful seaside views. The city’s diverse heritage is reflected in landmarks such as the Gangaramaya Temple, the Red Mosque, Independence Memorial Hall, and the historic Colombo Fort district.

Visitors can walk along Galle Face Green, explore the colorful streets of Pettah, and enjoy traditional Sri Lankan dishes such as rice and curry, hoppers, and kottu roti. Colombo also offers shopping centers, museums, restaurants, and a growing nightlife scene.

As Sri Lanka’s main transportation and business hub, Colombo is often the starting point for journeys across the country. Its energetic atmosphere, cultural diversity, and warm hospitality make it an engaging introduction to Sri Lanka.

counterfactuals.output:
**Suicide Blast Strikes Wattala as Sri Lankan Navy Reports Attack on LTTE Smuggling Boat**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka —** A suicide bomber detonated explosives on Sunday in Wattala, a heavily populated suburb north of Colombo, while the Sri Lankan navy separately said it had destroyed a vessel used by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam to smuggle weapons.

Police and military officials blamed the Wattala explosion on the LTTE, the separatist organization fighting to establish an independent Tamil state in northern and eastern Sri Lanka. Officials said the bomber struck near a security position, causing casualties among police or other security personnel and civilians in the surrounding area. Initial casualty reports varied as emergency teams transported the wounded to nearby hospitals.

Security forces sealed off the blast site, searched nearby buildings and questioned witnesses. Investigators were examining debris and body parts in an effort to identify the attacker and determine whether accomplices had helped with transport, reconnaissance or the preparation of the explosives.

Wattala lies just north of the capital and close to important roads, industrial areas and port facilities. The bombing highlighted the LTTE’s ability—or the authorities’ fear that it retained the ability—to carry out attacks well beyond the conventional front lines in the north.

Sri Lankan officials routinely described such attacks as attempts to create panic in and around Colombo at a time when government troops were pressing deeper into territory held by the Tigers. The LTTE generally did not immediately comment on individual bombings attributed to it.

In a separate announcement, the navy said one of its patrols had intercepted and destroyed an LTTE boat believed to be carrying weapons or military supplies. Naval officials said the vessel was detected in waters used by the Tigers’ maritime network and was sunk after a confrontation.

The military did not provide independently verifiable evidence of the boat’s cargo, and there was no immediate statement from the LTTE. Access to the war zone was tightly restricted, making claims by either side difficult to confirm.

The Tigers’ naval wing, known as the Sea Tigers, had long operated small, fast boats for combat, resupply and suicide attacks. The organization also developed an overseas procurement network to acquire explosives, ammunition and other military equipment. Sri Lanka’s navy made disrupting that network a central part of its strategy, announcing the destruction of several suspected arms vessels during the later stages of the war.

If confirmed, the loss of another smuggling craft would add to the pressure on the LTTE’s supply lines. Government forces were attempting to isolate Tiger-held areas, cut maritime routes and prevent reinforcements or weapons from reaching the rebels as the army advanced on land.

The two incidents illustrated the conflict’s parallel fronts. In the north, the government sought to defeat the LTTE through conventional military operations and a maritime blockade. Around Colombo, security agencies faced the continuing threat of bombings, infiltrators and clandestine cells.

The LTTE had fought the Sri Lankan state since the early 1980s, saying Tamils faced systematic discrimination under governments dominated by the Sinhalese majority. Over the course of the conflict, the group built a conventional army, a naval force and a suicide unit known as the Black Tigers. It was accused of assassinating political leaders and carrying out attacks against military and civilian targets.

Successive peace efforts failed, including a ceasefire signed in 2002. By the later years of the war, large-scale fighting had resumed, displacing civilians and producing growing international concern over access to food, medicine and safe areas.

After Sunday’s bombing, security was expected to tighten around Colombo and its northern approaches. Police urged residents to report suspicious people, vehicles and unattended packages, while investigators worked to establish how the attacker reached Wattala despite checkpoints and identity inspections.

Authorities presented the naval action as evidence that the LTTE was being steadily cut off from outside supplies. The suicide bombing, however, served as a reminder that even as the Tigers lost territory, they could still threaten locations far from the battlefield.

**Sri Lanka violence leaves scores dead as authorities pursue bombing suspects**

NEGOMBO, Sri Lanka — Sri Lankan security forces continued operations against suspected militants following coordinated Easter Sunday attacks that killed more than 250 people at churches and luxury hotels.

Among the deadliest attacks was a suicide bombing at St. Sebastian’s Church in Negombo, a predominantly Catholic city north of Colombo. Explosions also struck churches in Colombo and Batticaloa, as well as several hotels in the capital.

Authorities blamed a local Islamist extremist group, National Thowheed Jamath, and said the attackers had links to Islamic State, which claimed responsibility. Investigators have detained numerous suspects, although the extent of any direction or assistance from abroad remains under investigation.

Sri Lanka’s military said a subsequent raid in the eastern part of the country killed suspected militants and uncovered explosives and bomb-making materials. CNN could not independently verify the military’s account or its casualty figures.

The attacks reopened fears of large-scale violence in a country that endured nearly three decades of civil war. The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, commonly known as the Tamil Tigers or LTTE, fought to establish an independent state for ethnic Tamils in northern and eastern Sri Lanka. The group pioneered the use of suicide bombings and was accused of attacks on political leaders and civilian targets.

Government forces defeated the LTTE in May 2009, ending the war. Both sides were accused of serious human-rights violations, particularly during the conflict’s final months.

Authorities have not linked the Tamil Tigers to the Easter attacks. The reference to the LTTE reflects Sri Lanka’s history of political violence rather than evidence of involvement in the church and hotel bombings.
